PAPER VERSION 1 (4/7/2023, 2:19 PM):

Professor Davis
ENG101-0001
Question 2
	Fledgling, by Octavia Butler, deals immensely with this idea of bias against women and against certain races being coupled. Shori is a female vampire who has dark skin, and deals with trouble surrounding this throughout the entirety of the book. One might expect an imaginary world to be free of these problems, but Butler chooses to make a point by making them prominent in her fantasy world. In addition to these two things, Shori also has certain strifes that come strictly through being a vampire, burdening her more in certain cases. She deals with racism of all forms, spanning from subtle to blatant, and is disregarded in certain cases due to being a female. 
	Butler makes sure to avoid placing Shori too far out of reality in either direction, despite her status as a vampire. Shori is clearly smart and displays her mental strength in many cases. This comes in the form of mental durability in some instances, and problem solving in others. Butler avoids making her perfect however, as Shori is very prone to mistakes and questionable decisions throughout the story. This sense of humanity is confirmed in the fact that Shori’s Ina DNA is mixed with human DNA. Interestingly enough, this sometimes takes precedence over the racism within the book, such as in instances like where Wright says “Chances are, this is all happening for one of three reasons. It’s happening because some human group has spotted your kind and decided you’re all dangerous, evil vampires. Or it’s happening because some Ina group or Ina individual is jealous of the success Shori’s family had with blending human and Ina DNA and having children who can stay awake through the day and not burn so easily in the sun. Or it’s happening because Shori is black, and racists—probably Ina racists—don’t like the idea that a good part of the answer to your daytime problems is melanin” (Butler 153).
	This begs the question of the role of these racist ideas within the book. They exist despite not necessarily needing to, but aren’t always at the forefront. Though sometimes not obvious, this provides an overall commentary from Butler on the issue at hand. Shori has moments of struggle caused by dealing with being a woman of color, but these instances don’t define her. Butler could have avoided including this idea, or had a grand way in which they were fought, or rather, didn’t affect Shori. Instead, their inclusion but occasional lack of prominence mirrors the real world. Shori isn’t above these problems, as they weigh on her in this fictional world just as they do for many in the real world, but they don’t drag her completely down. Butler uses this to reflect modern society, and make an overall point about persevering through these unfair notions, claiming an identity outside of them.


Question 3
	Salt Fish Girl, by Larissa Lai, is a great example of how style and form can be used creatively in the world of science fiction in order to create meaning. The book details the story of Nu Wa and Miranda, who are two different versions of one girl, living at different times. These stories intertwine with each other, but Laai also does so with ease, avoiding jarring transitions while developing the same character in two different timelines. This creates the feeling of two separate stories, all while building towards one overall narrative and inevitable conclusion.
	At the beginning of one of Miranda’s sections, she says “My parents were so anxious about my odour, I didn’t tell them about the scales, which didn’t appear at the bottom of the tub with much frequency anyway. For all the years of my childhood, not a month went by without a secret trip to some doctor’s office or herbalist’s shop in the Unregulated Zone” (Lai 59). Lai dives directly back into Miranda’s story, avoiding a blatant transition of any sort. This emphasizes this creation of two different stories, despite the reader obviously knowing it all takes place in the same book, creating clear correlation. Creating a clear divide by doing this gives the reader the opportunity to know these two characters separately, as Lai intends, which is necessary to the plot of the story. This creates an unique experience for the reader, and works well with different aspects of science fiction which are essential to the plot. 
	This separation of story into two different timelines and characters creates an obvious fantasy-based setting, acclimating the reader to a world of fantasy. This allows Lai to easily place her reader into the story, meaning she can casually imply other important story elements, such as Miranda’s smell, her scales, and the “Unregulated Zone,” all mentioned in the previous quote. This immersive style of storytelling gives Lai the ability to focus on developing the characters and story, without having to explain each imaginative detail time and time again. It also bridges the gap to more inventive ideas, such as work being in the form of a video game. Lai fully embraces the world of science fiction to create her narrative, and exemplifies her willingness to take unique storytelling approaches in order to do so.


Question 4
	Oryx and Crake by Margaret Atwood and Brown Girl in the Ring by Nalo Hopkinson both portray dystopian post-apocalyptic societies in their stories, but in vastly different ways. Oryx and Crake tells the story of Snowman, who appears to be in a state of desolation both mentally and physically. One of the earliest descriptions we get of him comes from himself in saying “He stands up and raises his arms to stretch, and his sheet falls off. He looks down at his body with dismay: the grimy, bugbitten skin, the salt-and-pepper tufts of hair, the thickening yellow toenails” (Atwood 11). His physical state often mirrors his mental state, and the state of the world around him. We also see the futuristic setting of the world before the deadly pandemic, with a significant part of the story being Crake’s different schemes which are slowly revealed. Snowman has to scavenge in order to survive, and has a distant yet active relationship with the Crakers. The entire setting places an emphasis on survival, all while pointing towards how the world has crashed and burned around Snowman.
Contrary to Oryx and Crake, much of Brown Girl in the Ring takes place in what was once urban areas. Hopkinson describes this crash in an apocalyptic state by saying “When Toronto’s economic base collapsed, investors, commerce, and government withdrew into the suburb cities, leaving the rotten core to decay. Those who stayed were the ones who couldn’t or wouldn’t leave” (Hopkinson 6). Ti-Jeanne spends much of her time at home with family, mainly taking care of her baby. While still survival based, this story of this book exists in a very different setting. These characters are fighting for their survival from villainous characters, and much of the action takes place on a spiritual level. Rather than characters coming together in order to survive in trying times, this story shows different characters abusing the post-apocalyptic social dynamic, aiming to amass as much power as they possibly can.
These differing dystopian settings have a clear impact on how the main characters operate. Fighting for his survival in very deserted areas, Snowman has clearly become self-centered to a certain degree. He doesn’t really think before he speaks, and many of his comments and actions are somewhat primal. Alternatively, Ti-Jeanne is still surrounded by family, and still somewhat connected with a modern setting around her, even if it has collapsed. She’s still mindful of other people, and cares for her family members, even when they make it difficult. Another major aspect of their different mentalities is the state of their company. Ti-Jeanne is still surrounded by loved ones, while Snowman is all alone besides the Crakers, who he can’t fully connect with. These environments drive the characters in different directions. Snowman is often hard to root for, while Ti-Jeanne is far easier to connect with. Despite sharing the basis of a dystopian post-apocalyptic setting focused on survival, these stories and characters are driven in extremely different directions based on the specifics of their situation.  


Question 5
Susana Morris’ article “Black Girls Are from the Future: Afrofuturistic Feminism in Octavia E. Butler’s Fledgling,” aligns perfectly with these questions. Morris breaks down the genre of science fiction, as well as its constraints, upsides, and the ways in which it's progressing. In it, Morris assesses the role of black women in science fiction, but also relates it to the fundamental ideas of the genre as a whole. While science fiction seems limitless, stories and characters often fall into the same holes over and over, even aligning with real world stereotypes, despite existing within an imaginary reality. We see these common tropes having to be broken down by authors willing to blaze a new trail, as Morris points out in saying that Fledgling “revises the contemporary vampire genre by reconfiguring the trope of the vampire from enchanted icon of whiteness to consider how race, sexuality, and intimacy can function in potentially progressive ways” (Morris 146-147). 
These repetitively used storylines limit science fiction, countering the point of the genre as a whole. Science fiction opens the doors to endless possibilities, as anything is fair game due to the nature of these texts. Regarding Atwood’s claims, science fiction does allow us to explore new technologies, as readers can envision them within their own lives, while also contemplating the potential downfalls. With no limitations on characters, the idea of what a human is can be brought into question, and evaluated in each specific piece. The role of humanity within the universe, as well as religion, mythology, and so on, can be brought into question, or completely altered depending on the text. Changes in social dynamics and organizations can be investigated, and potentially deemed necessary in some instances depending on the experience of a reader. The imagination can be pushed for both author and reader, as the lack of true barriers means pondering ideas that may have never previously been considered. Science fiction promotes creativity, in that the absence of restrictions presents the opportunity to go where no one has gone before. 
The claims being made by both Atwood and Morris are true, but these opportunities mean nothing without agency in order to take advantage of them. Endless options for the creative mind mean nothing if story after story follows the line of the exact same trope. The abundance of possibilities has to be taken advantage of, rather than transferring stereotypes into an imaginative world, only to let them dictate there as well. As Morris points out, Octavia Butler uses her characters in Fledgling to break free of theme norms, and sets her brand of science fiction on a course that takes advantage of these elements mentioned by Atwood. All of these ideas put forth by Atwood are possible within the world of science fiction, but they can’t be made true on their own. Similar to the real world, it’s easy to follow along with society and put forth what the world is used to seeing. A true difference is made when someone breaks free from the ordinary, and takes action to create something new, be it challenging what’s standard in the real world, or pushing the limits of fictional ones. 

Works Cited
Atwood, Margaret. “Oryx and Crake.” Knopf Doubleday Publishing Group, MaddAddam Trilogy, Book 1, 2003, p. 11. Kindle Edition.
Butler, Octavia E.. “Fledgling.” Seven Stories Press, 2005, p. 153. Kindle Edition. 
Hopkinson, Nalo. “Brown Girl in the Ring.” Grand Central Publishing, 1998, p.6. Kindle Edition. 
Lai, Larissa. “Salt Fish Girl.” Thomas Island Publishers, 2002, p.59. 
Morris, Susana. “Black Girls Are from the Future: Afrofuturistic Feminism in Octavia E. Butler’s Fledgling.” Women’s Studies Quarterly, vol. 40, no. 3/4, The Feminist Press at the City University of New York, 2012, pp. 146-166.

Professor Miller
ENG202-0002
QName
	William Shakespeare is known for his vast array of works that shaped the culture of his day, so much so that his impact has carried over to our modern world in countless ways. Despite each story being noticeably different, Shakespeare had many themes that carried over from play to play. One of the most obvious is that of redemption. From grand heroes to despicable villains, many characters had a redemptive storyline through their narrative in Shakespeare’s stories, whether they were seeking it or not. Conversely, many characters fell short of redemption, with their story ending while their characters were still in a very questionable moral state. Shakespeare is known for carefully crafting each and every story, so one would assume that there is some degree of intention behind having a heavy emphasis on redemption throughout multiple stories. Additionally, there is also a bulk of information we can gain about who Shakespeare was as a person by dissecting these themes and storylines. The inconsistency between characters who do and don’t get their redemption may seem haphazard, but this actually eludes to another theme Shakespeare highlights, which is fate.
	Redemption for villainous characters is one of the most common storylines we see in entertainment, spanning from the time of Shakespeare all the way up to our modern culture. Sometimes this was done in very obvious ways, such as with Prospero in the Tempest. Prospero was completely set on revenge through the early portion of the story, but slowly turned to forgiveness as the play progressed, resulting in a total turnaround as a character. Sometimes these moments of redemption are less clear, as is true for Edmund in King Lear, who admits to ordering the death of Lear and Cordelia, and attempts to go back on his command, despite it being too late. This is a far less obvious reversal of character’s morals, and can be interpreted in a variety of ways. Edmund is unbelievably malevolent at points, but also “justifies his evil actions to achieve restoring his rightful position by climbing out of the discriminatory condition he is born into” (Nilay). This leaves the reader to question the final moral state of his character, a discussion which Shakespeare readers should be accustomed to.
	While it may be a more centralized theme for more wicked characters, redemption isn’t specific to solely villains. There are plenty of characters who make questionable decisions and then focus on correcting their mistakes, despite not being an evil character. In Romeo and Juliet, Romeo kills Tybalt to avenge his dear friend Mercutio. Most would agree that Romeo isn’t a villain, but there is a sense of redemption in the fact that Romeo ends up dying at the end of the play. In fact, all of the trouble that stirs because of this love story is balanced out by their eventual unfortunate demise. It may not be a heartwarming moment of redemption for the “star-crossed lovers,” but it is a fitting conclusion to their story. Redemption isn’t always the choice of the character, but rather is sewn into the plot in whatever way is deemed best by Shakespeare. Villains are more frequently in need of this redemption, but that doesn’t make it exclusive.
	This also brings up questions regarding a lack of redemption for both. Many characters get an ideal or fitting ending to their storyline, but the story for many just ends, seemingly with no real intention. 

Works Cited
Atwood, Margaret. “Oryx and Crake.” Knopf Doubleday Publishing Group, MaddAddam Trilogy, Book 1, 2003, p. 11. Kindle Edition.
Butler, Octavia E.. “Fledgling.” Seven Stories Press, 2005, p. 153. Kindle Edition. 
Hopkinson, Nalo. “Brown Girl in the Ring.” Grand Central Publishing, 1998, p.6. Kindle Edition. 
Lai, Larissa. “Salt Fish Girl.” Thomas Island Publishers, 2002, p.59. 
Morris, Susana. “Black Girls Are from the Future: Afrofuturistic Feminism in Octavia E. Butler’s Fledgling.” Women’s Studies Quarterly, vol. 40, no. 3/4, The Feminist Press at the City University of New York, 2012, pp. 146-166.

Most would agree that Romeo isn’t a villain, but there is a sense of redemption in the fact that Romeo ends up dying at the end of the play. Villains are more frequently in need of this redemption, but that doesn’t make it exclusive.
	This also brings up questions regarding a lack of redemption for both. Many characters get an ideal or fitting ending to their storyline, but the story for many just ends, seemingly with no real intention. Even ones who ideally would get some form of redemption, having serious yet correctable flaws, see the conclusion of their story met with no discernable change. Malvolio from Twelfth Night is an example of this, as he remains somewhat constant throughout the entire story. Despite being widely disliked within the story, Malvolio’s egotistic nature continues on, devoid of any real change before the story’s conclusion. While it may seem cruel for some characters to be left morally uncorrected, it provides a sense of variation that Shakespeare's plays would lack if every questionable character was met with the same story arc.
	Aside from assessing how different character types find or lack redemption, it’s necessary to examine how the theme differs within Shakespeare’s two main types of stories. The large majority of Shakespeare’s works can either be categorized as a tragedy, or a comedy. Comedies are more upbeat and comedic with most characters having a happy fitting ending, while tragedies have a serious tone, and are riddled with death at the story’s conclusion. Starting with comedies, one might argue that redemption is necessary to a complete happy ending. Loose ends of the plot can be tied up, but the story will likely still feel incomplete without the progression of characters to satisfy the audience. This isn’t necessarily always true, but allowing main characters to find redemption is a powerful plot device, especially for creating a warm feeling to conclude a story. Despite it seeming necessary to the ideal conclusion of a comedy, we see increased emphasis on this idea in tragedies, as they typically include more severe storylines and endings.
	Redemption is a crucial idea in tragedies, but in a very different way. Instead of correcting characters in order to have a happy ending, the redeemed characters in these stories are likely acting on their final opportunity to make things right before meeting their untimely demise. This makes for a more grave situation, especially given the themes of spirituality we see through most of Shakespeare’s plays. Not only are these characters being judged by the others within the story, but they’re being looked at by God, through whatever role Shakespeare seems fit for it to play. These plays were meant to be captivating, meaning Shakespare intended for audience members to become enveloped and begin to judge characters in this way themselves. This only increases the importance of redemption for these characters, as their final actions will determine the type of legacy they leave on the story. Tragedies often conclude with many deaths from relevant characters, meaning these concluding moments are highly analyzed, as they are known to be their last, even beyond the confines of a play’s allotted time.
	Similar to how some heroes and villains never get their redemption in these stories, both tragedies and comedies lack redemption in certain instances. Some believe that King Lear is an example of this, as it concludes with almost everyone perishing, while some characters are still in very questionable states, and make little progress regarding reparation. In the article "Sin, Suffering, and Redemption in ‘Leir’ and ‘Lear’” Stephen Lynch notes this in saying “several modern commentators think the ending so desolate that they interpret it as an expression of nihilism, claiming that whatever love and joy Lear and Cordelia attain proves a mere illusion snatched away by a world devoid of moral order” (Lynch).

Works Cited
Atwood, Margaret. “Oryx and Crake.” Knopf Doubleday Publishing Group, MaddAddam Trilogy, Book 1, 2003, p. 11. Kindle Edition.
Butler, Octavia E.. “Fledgling.” Seven Stories Press, 2005, p. 153. Kindle Edition. 
Hopkinson, Nalo. “Brown Girl in the Ring.” Grand Central Publishing, 1998, p.6. Kindle Edition. 
Lai, Larissa. “Salt Fish Girl.” Thomas Island Publishers, 2002, p.59. 
Morris, Susana. “Black Girls Are from the Future: Afrofuturistic Feminism in Octavia E. Butler’s Fledgling.” Women’s Studies Quarterly, vol. 40, no. 3/4, The Feminist Press at the City University of New York, 2012, pp. 146-166.

This debate is common in regards to Edmund’s death, as he could have attempted to reverse his order, knowing all too well that it couldn’t be done. The Inescapability of Fate in Shakespeare’s Portrayal of Redemption
	William Shakespeare is known for his vast array of works that shaped the culture of his day, so much so that his impact has carried over to our modern world in countless ways. Additionally, there is also a bulk of information we can gain about who Shakespeare was as a person by dissecting these themes and storylines. The inconsistency between characters who do and don’t get their redemption may seem haphazard, but this actually eludes to another theme Shakespeare highlights, which is fate.
	Redemption for villainous characters is one of the most common storylines we see in entertainment, spanning from the time of Shakespeare all the way up to our modern culture. Sometimes this was done in very obvious ways, such as with Prospero in the Tempest. Prospero was completely set on revenge through the early portion of the story, but slowly turned to forgiveness as the play progressed, resulting in a total turnaround as a character. Sometimes these moments of redemption are less clear, as is true for Edmund in King Lear, who admits to ordering the death of Lear and Cordelia, and attempts to go back on his command, despite it being too late. This is a far less obvious reversal of a character’s morals, and can be interpreted in a variety of ways. Edmund is unbelievably malevolent at points, but also “justifies his evil actions to achieve restoring his rightful position by climbing out of the discriminatory condition he is born into” (Nilay). This leaves the reader to question the final moral state of his character, a discussion which Shakespeare readers should be accustomed to.
	While it may be a centralized theme for more wicked characters, redemption isn’t specific to solely villains. There are plenty of characters who make questionable decisions and then focus on correcting their mistakes, despite not being an evil character. In Romeo and Juliet, Romeo kills Tybalt to avenge his dear friend Mercutio. Most would agree that Romeo isn’t a villain, but there is a sense of redemption in the fact that Romeo ends up dying at the end of the play. In fact, all of the trouble that stirs because of this love story is balanced out by their eventual unfortunate demise. It may not be a heartwarming moment of redemption for the “star-crossed lovers,” but it is a fitting conclusion to their story. Redemption isn’t always the choice of the character, but rather is sewn into the plot in whatever way is deemed best by Shakespeare. Villains are more frequently in need of this redemption, but that doesn’t make it exclusive.
	This also brings up questions regarding a lack of redemption for both. Many characters get an ideal or fitting ending to their storyline, but the story for many just ends, seemingly with no real intention. Even ones who ideally would get some form of redemption, having serious yet correctable flaws, see the conclusion of their story met with no discernable change. Malvolio from Twelfth Night is an example of this, as he remains somewhat constant throughout the entire story. Despite being widely disliked within the play, Malvolio’s egotistic nature continues on, devoid of any real change before the story’s conclusion. While it may seem cruel for some characters to be left morally uncorrected, it provides a sense of variation that Shakespeare's plays would lack if every questionable character was met with the same story arc.
	Aside from assessing how different character types find or lack redemption, it’s necessary to examine how themes differ within Shakespeare’s two main types of stories. The large majority of Shakespeare’s works can be categorized as either a tragedy, or a comedy. Comedies are more upbeat and romanticized with most characters having a happy fitting ending, while tragedies have a serious tone, and are riddled with death at the story’s conclusion. Starting with comedies, one might argue that redemption is necessary to a complete happy ending. Loose ends within the plot can be tied up, but the story will likely still feel incomplete without the progression of characters to satisfy the audience. This isn’t necessarily always true, but allowing main characters to find redemption is a powerful plot device, especially for creating a warm feeling to conclude a story. Despite it seeming necessary to the ideal conclusion of a comedy, we see increased emphasis on this idea in tragedies, as they typically include more severe storylines and endings.
	Redemption is a crucial idea in tragedies, but in a very different way. Instead of correcting characters in order to have a happy ending, the redeemed characters in these stories are likely acting on their final opportunity to make things right before meeting their untimely demise. This makes for a more grave situation, especially given the themes of spirituality we see throughout most of Shakespeare’s plays. Not only are these characters being examined by the others within the story, but they’re being looked at by God, in accordance with whatever role Shakespeare seems fit for this judgment to play. These plays were meant to be captivating, meaning Shakespare intended for audience members to become enveloped and begin to judge characters in this way themselves. This only increases the importance of redemption for these characters, as their final actions will determine the type of legacy they leave on the story. Tragedies often conclude with many deaths from relevant characters, meaning these concluding moments are highly analyzed, as they are known to be their last, even beyond the confines of a play’s allotted time.
	Similar to how some heroes and villains never get their redemption in these stories, both tragedies and comedies lack redemption in certain instances. Some believe that King Lear is an example of this, as it concludes with almost everyone perishing, while some characters are still in very questionable states, and make little progress regarding reparation. In the article "Sin, Suffering, and Redemption in ‘Leir’ and ‘Lear’” Stephen Lynch notes this in saying “several modern commentators think the ending so desolate that they interpret it as an expression of nihilism, claiming that whatever love and joy Lear and Cordelia attain proves a mere illusion snatched away by a world devoid of moral order” (Lynch). Desolation is evident in the play’s conclusion, but this doesn’t necessarily indicate a nihilistic message. Rather, Shakespeare plays into the idea of fate once again, all while continuing to prioritize fluctuation in his storytelling. He fends off predictability within his writing and makes a point by indicating that blatant redemption for everyone simply isn’t a realistic idea, even within the bounds of a story. This emphasizes a certain sense of realism, not to suggest that everyone can’t be redeemed, but that it won’t be found simply out of convenience, with no effort from the troubled soul.
	While some characters are lucky enough to be redeemed with little to no effort on their part, Shakespeare doesn’t allow this to be the reality for most. Typically characters find this after some degree of agency on their part, where they start to realize the effects of their actions and seek change accordingly, be it in the moment, or later on. Something that frequently sets this off is a sense of guilt or remorse that eventually pushes the character to try and change, and make reparations for their actions. This is sometimes difficult to point out, as it can be hard to draw the line between true remorse, and simply wanting to seem like a mended individual, without any actualized changes in behavior. This debate is common in regards to Edmund’s death, as he could have attempted to reverse his order, knowing all too well that it couldn’t be done.  This complicates the idea even further, and leaves certain storylines up to audience discretion, differing based on personal thoughts and moral stand points.
	This traces back to the intention behind all of this, which is to entertain an audience. Calling these questions to the attention of an audience not only keeps them mentally stimulated, but likely ensures future engagement as well. These plays provided a way for people to escape reality, as they became invested in these different worlds sculpted in Shakespeare’s mind. These redemptive story lines provided complete character arcs for audiences to become invested in, but also left them wanting more when they were missing. Not following the same plot lines with every single play brought in a sense of realism, meaning audiences were more likely to connect with what they were watching. Instead of knowing exactly what was going to happen, audiences were hooked by waiting to see if certain characters would morally reform before the play’s end. Not only could Shakespeare make a point with these storylines, but he could manipulate audience reaction based on what he chose to include. He learned what audiences responded well to, and focused on infusing that with whatever message he was intending to convey.
	Part of what made Shakespeare so renowned and successful was his ability to craft a point he intended to make, and develop it into a work that audiences would come and intently watch. This may have been easier to do with more straightforward heroes and villains, but Shakespeare sought to convey his message in a less simplistic manner, in order to more effectively drive the point home. As pointed out by Jennifer Staehle in “Shakespeare ‘s Evil: From Vice to Villain,” his characters aren’t “one-dimensional vice figures that are obviously evil. Instead, Shakespeare bestows vice-like qualities within a human, thus adding to the evolution of evil as Shakespeare portrays the villain as having potential for both good and evil because that is the state of mankind: somewhere between good and evil” (Staehle). He used his villains and their pursuit of redemption to comment on the reality of society’s outlook on perfection. He used them to characterize this gray area between good and evil, and the reality of inconsistency regarding fate for those in it. 
	With so much variation regarding which characters end up having a moment of redemption, it calls to mind questions about how random the decision making was for Shakespeare. We’ve seen lesser characters get redemption as compared to those who truly needed it, or those who audiences believe deserved it more. Some sorrowful characters have only seen their redemption actualized in that emotion, while others’ mistakes are fully rectified. This may seem random, but it ties in perfectly with the focal point of fate that Shakespeare so heavily emphasizes. The end results won’t always make perfect sense, and the characters who need redemption the most won’t always get it. Shakespeare indicates a lack of human understanding, suggesting through these stories that plans often don’t go as intended. Not every story ends when it's expected to, meaning they won’t always conclude with a well-crafted culmination of everything leading up to it. This is even more of a reality for people in the real world, never knowing what may be in store as time progresses.
	Shakespeare uses redemption as a storytelling device, but also to provide commentary on the fate of those in the real world. His variation between each play helps captivate audiences through an element of mystery, while also playing into the idea of an individual's story not always going as anticipated. Shakespeare created narratives in an attempt to enlighten his audience, while still concocting plays that kept crowds on their toes. Shakespeare himself wasn’t perfect, and he represented this in his writing by not confining characters within the limitations of classic heroic or villainous tropes. Instead he affirmed the fallibility of humanity and their necessary longing for redemption, all while insinuating that fate isn’t a storyteller like himself.
